lesson.title: Standard Deviation: Measuring the Typical Distance from the Mean
lesson.summary: The standard deviation summarizes spread by measuring, in the original units of the data, roughly how far a typical observation lies from the mean, using every value in the data set rather than just the extremes.
lesson.body:
The range only looks at the two most extreme values, which throws away almost everything you know about a distribution. Standard deviation fixes that by using every single observation. The core idea is to measure how far each data value sits from the mean, and then combine all of those distances into one typical distance. Because it is built directly from the mean, standard deviation only makes sense once you can already compute a mean, and it is the standard way statisticians describe how spread out a distribution is.

The calculation has a specific shape for a good reason. First you find each value's deviation from the mean, value minus mean, which can be positive or negative. If you simply averaged these deviations, the positives and negatives would cancel out to zero for any data set, telling you nothing. So each deviation is squared first, which makes every term positive and also gives more weight to values that are far from the mean than to values that are close. These squared deviations are averaged, using a specific divisor covered fully when calculating variance, and finally you take a square root to undo the squaring and return to the original units of the data.

Take the five values 4, 8, 6, 5, and 3. Their mean is 4 plus 8 plus 6 plus 5 plus 3, divided by 5, which is 26 divided by 5, or 5.2. The deviations from the mean are -1.2, 2.8, 0.8, -0.2, and -2.2. Squaring each deviation gives 1.44, 7.84, 0.64, 0.04, and 4.84, which sum to 14.8. Treating this as a sample and dividing by n minus 1, which is 4, gives a variance of 3.7. Taking the square root of 3.7 gives a standard deviation of approximately 1.92. That 1.92 is measured in the same units as the original data, so you can say a typical value sits about 1.92 units away from the mean of 5.2.

That last property, staying in the original units, is what makes standard deviation so much more interpretable than the squared quantity used along the way. A standard deviation of 1.92 test points, or 1.92 centimeters, or 1.92 dollars, means something concrete: it is comparable in scale to the data itself. This is also why standard deviation, not variance, is the number usually reported alongside a mean, and why it becomes the building block for z-scores, which measure how many standard deviations a specific value lies from the mean.

Like the mean, standard deviation is not resistant. Because it is built from squared distances to the mean, and the mean itself shifts with outliers, a single extreme value can inflate the standard deviation dramatically, often more than it inflates the mean. That tradeoff, sensitivity in exchange for using all the information in the data, is exactly why statisticians pair standard deviation with resistant measures like the median and the interquartile range when a distribution might be skewed or contain outliers.
